metadata.title: The assessment of collaborative problem solving in PISA 2015: An investigation of the validity of the PISA 2015 CPS tasks

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a recruited, school-based sample in Germany (35 ninth- and 10th-grade classes) rather than the full international PISA sampling frame. The analysis relied on structural equation modeling in MPlus (type=complex for nested students within classes) and response surface analysis in R; the manuscript does not report applying PISA-style student sampling weights or replicate weights. Because the paper focuses on construct/predictive validity of CPS task scores within a convenience sample, no explicit weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is documented. The main data preparation steps described are task subsampling (four of seven CPS tasks; exclusion of the reformatted H–H00 version) and aggregation of CPS task points into four indicators for latent modeling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are not PISA cognitive achievement PV-based scores; instead, the study uses CPS task performance scores (aggregated task indicators) and other test measures (reasoning sum scores, reading manifest score) plus collaboration questionnaire factors. Missing-data handling is not reported in the provided text: while the teacher questionnaire includes missing values (n=64 missing values for teaching time), the manuscript does not specify whether missing responses were imputed, excluded, or handled via full-information methods. This omission limits reproducibility of the analytic sample definition for the latent and regression models.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Recruited students from eight German secondary public schools (Gymnasium) in Rhineland-Palatinate and Hesse; ensured participants had not taken the main PISA 2015 CPS tasks previously. Administered only four of the seven original PISA 2015 CPS tasks (four individual-player tasks and one face-to-face co-player task), and excluded students who completed only the reformatted H–H00 version (replacing one computer agent with a real classmate). For the co-player predictive validity analysis, integrated only one partner per group to avoid identical dyad scores, yielding N=228 observed individual scores used in Model C.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) tasks (German H-A format), grades 9-10, Germany
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model A (SEM, MPlus type=complex): χ2=778.649, df=655, p<.01, CFI=0.914, TLI=0.908, RMSEA=0.020; latent correlations: self-reported collaboration r=0.25 (p<.001), teacher-reported collaboration r=0.33 (p<.001). Model B: χ2=928.850, df=807, p<.01, CFI=0.918, TLI=0.912, RMSEA=0.018; latent correlations: self-reported collaboration r=0.29 (p<.001), teacher-reported collaboration r=0.20 (p<.05), reasoning r=0.38 (p<.001), CPS-reading relation r=0.29 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 CPS tasks (German H-A format) the study leveraged self-reported collaboration and teacher-reported collaboration to predict PISA 2015 CPS performance, finding that CPS performance was moderately associated with both self-reported collaboration (r≈0.25–0.29) and teacher-reported collaboration (r≈0.20–0.33). This indicates that the H-A CPS task scores show construct validity against external collaboration evaluations, supporting the use of PISA 2015 CPS tasks for measuring collaborative problem-solving skills, though the evidence is associative rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) tasks (German co-player format), grades 9-10, Germany
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model C (response surface analysis; RSQD): AIC=2975.41, CFI=1.00; explained variance=30.2%. Significant effects in RSQD: students’ CPS main effect β=0.31 (p<.001), partners’ CPS main effect β=0.26 (p<.001), interaction effect β=-0.12 (p=0.038), squared effect of students’ CPS β=-0.11 (p=0.020); squared effect of partners’ CPS not significant β=-0.08 (p=0.078).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 CPS tasks (German co-player format) the study leveraged students’ CPS performance and partner CPS performance to predict joint co-player CPS performance, finding that dyad outcomes depended on both partners’ individual CPS levels with a significant interaction and nonlinear (squared) student effect. This indicates that individual CPS scores from the H-A tasks have predictive validity for collaborative performance in a structurally similar co-player setting, supporting policy and practice decisions that treat CPS task performance as meaningful for team-based problem solving, while noting that the study is limited to a small German convenience sample and does not record actual interaction processes.

data.outcome_summary: This study recruited 483 German secondary-school students (grades 9–10) from eight Gymnasium schools in Rhineland-Palatinate and Hesse to evaluate the validity of PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving (CPS) tasks. Students completed four of the seven original PISA 2015 CPS tasks in an individual-player H–A format, and a fifth CPS task in a co-player (face-to-face) format with a randomly assigned classmate; the co-player predictive analysis used one partner per dyad (N=228 observed individual scores). Construct validity was tested with SEM in MPlus (type=complex for students nested in classes), showing moderate associations between CPS performance and self-reported collaboration (r≈0.25–0.29) and teacher-reported collaboration (r≈0.20–0.33), with reasoning showing a robust relation (r≈0.38). Predictive validity was assessed via response surface analysis (RSQD), explaining 30.2% of co-player performance variance and revealing significant main and interaction effects of individual CPS performance. Limitations include the associative nature of results (no causal inference), a small non-PISA sampling frame, and missing-data handling not being specified in the provided text.
